overview:
Haribhadra’s yoga refers primarily to the Jain philosophical and practical system of yoga articulated by Ācārya Haribhadrasūri (often dated between the 6th and 8th centuries CE), especially in his Sanskrit work Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya (“Compendium of Yoga Views”) and the shorter Prakrit text Yogaviṁśikā (“Twenty Verses on Yoga”). Haribhadra is a Śvetāmbara Jain thinker who stands at a crucial crossroads of Indian intellectual history: he is deeply rooted in Jain doctrine, yet engages extensively with Buddhist and Brahmanical (especially Sāṃkhya–Yoga and Vedānta) traditions. His yoga is therefore both distinctly Jain and consciously comparative.

In Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya, Haribhadra defines yoga in broad, soteriological terms as that which is conducive to liberation (mokṣa). Rather than restricting yoga to physical postures or a single school, he surveys multiple “views” (dṛṣṭis) and practices of yoga found among Buddhists, Hindus, and Jains, and then organizes them into an eightfold Jain framework. This eightfold scheme—Mitrā, Tārā, Balā, Dīprā, Sthirā, Kāntā, Prabhā, and Parā—maps the progressive refinement of the practitioner’s ethical character, meditative discipline, and spiritual insight. Haribhadra correlates these stages with the traditional Jain doctrine of the fourteen guṇasthānas (stages of spiritual development), emphasizing especially the gradual weakening and eventual eradication of mohanīya-karma (deluding karma).

Haribhadra’s yoga is also notable for its explicit dialogue with Patañjali’s Yogasūtra. He compares his eight yogas with Patañjali’s eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga-yoga: yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, samādhi), a Buddhist yoga attributed to Bhadanta Bhāskara, and a Vedānta-oriented system attributed to Bandhu Bhagavaddatta. In doing so, he neither simply adopts nor rejects these systems; instead, he reinterprets them through a Jain lens. For example, Mitrā is associated with respectful emulation of the wise (akin to yama), Tārā with service and observance (niyama), Balā with control of posture and passions (āsana), Dīprā with regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma), Sthirā with inward withdrawal (pratyāhāra), Kāntā with concentration (dhāraṇā), Prabhā with meditative absorption (dhyāna), and Parā with the highest realization comparable to samādhi.

A distinctive feature of Haribhadra’s yoga is his theological and philosophical pluralism. He insists that while liberated beings (whether described as possessing mokṣa, nirvāṇa, or kevala-jñāna) are spoken of differently in various traditions, their teachings are grounded in a common truth. He famously remarks that perhaps the teaching is one, but it shines forth in various ways because different people hear it, and that there cannot be a single road to different cities. This pluralistic stance does not dilute his Jain identity; rather, it allows him to affirm the value of multiple paths while maintaining the Jain emphasis on non-violence (ahiṃsā), right faith (samyagdarśana), right knowledge (samyagjñāna), and right conduct (samyakcāritra).

Within the broader Jain yoga tradition, Haribhadra’s contribution marks a shift from earlier, more strictly doctrinal presentations of meditation and spiritual practice toward a systematized, cross-traditional theory of yoga. He integrates canonical Jain notions such as adhyātma (inner spirituality), bhāvanā (contemplation), dhyāna (meditation), svādhyāya (scriptural study), and saṃyama (self-restraint) into a graded path that can be compared with non-Jain yogas without collapsing their differences. Later Jain authors, including Hemacandra and modern teachers, draw on Haribhadra’s framework when discussing Jain yoga in relation to other Indian philosophies.

In contemporary scholarship, Haribhadra’s yoga is studied both as a key source for Jain meditation theory and as an important document of Indian comparative philosophy. His careful analysis of liberation, the nature of the liberated soul, and omniscience, along with his critique of sectarianism and “logic-chopping,” continues to inform modern discussions about religious pluralism, inter-traditional dialogue, and the ethical foundations of spiritual practice. For students of Jainism, Haribhadra’s yoga offers a bridge between classical doctrinal formulations and a more dialogical, philosophically expansive vision of the path to liberation.

primary_sources.title: Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Haribhadrasūri
primary_sources.original_text:
नत्वेच्छा योगतोऽयोगं योगिगम्यं जिनोत्तमं वीरं

यद्येकं शिक्षणं स्यादपि नानाविधं श्रुतं जनानाम्
अचिन्त्यपुण्यप्रभावाद् विविधं प्रकाशते तदेव

न हि भिन्ननगराणां मार्गोऽपि कदाचिदेक एव
primary_sources.transliteration:
natvecchā yogato ’yogaṃ yogigamyaṃ jinottamaṃ vīraṃ

yad ekaṃ śikṣaṇaṃ syād api nānāvidhaṃ śrutaṃ janānām
acintya-puṇya-prabhāvād vividhaṃ prakāśate tadeva

na hi bhinna-nagarāṇāṃ mārgo ’pi kadācid eka eva
primary_sources.translation:
“Taking recourse to what is technically called ‘yoga by intention’, I bow to Vīra (Mahāvīra), the supreme victor, who is free from all bodily, mental, and vocal activity, and who is accessible only to yogins.

Perhaps the teaching is one, yet it is heard in various ways by different people; on account of the inconceivable power of merit, that very teaching shines forth in diverse forms.

There could never be a single road to different cities.”
primary_sources.notes: Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya is a 228-verse Sanskrit treatise on Jain yoga. The benedictory verse invokes Mahāvīra and introduces Haribhadra’s pluralistic outlook: a single liberating teaching manifests in multiple traditions. The text systematically compares Jain, Buddhist, and Brahmanical yogas, organizing them into eight progressive yoga-views (dṛṣṭis) aligned with Jain soteriology and the guṇasthāna framework.

primary_sources.title: Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya (Eightfold Jain Yoga)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Haribhadrasūri
primary_sources.original_text:
मित्रा तारा च बला दीप्रा स्थिरा कान्ता प्रभा परा चेति
अष्टौ योगदृष्टयः प्रोक्ता मोक्षोपायाः क्रमोन्नताः

मित्रा यमसमन्विता तारा नियमार्चिता बलाासनसंयुता
दीप्रा प्राणविनिग्रहस्थिरा प्रत्याहारलक्षणा कान्ता धारणा
प्रभा ध्यानसमन्विता परा तु समाधिकथिता
primary_sources.transliteration:
mitrā tārā ca balā dīprā sthirā kāntā prabhā parā ceti
aṣṭau yogadṛṣṭayaḥ proktā mokṣopāyāḥ kramonnatāḥ

mitrā yama-samanvitā tārā niyamārcitā balā āsana-saṃyutā
dīprā prāṇa-vinigraha sthirā pratyāhāra-lakṣaṇā kāntā dhāraṇā
prabhā dhyāna-samanvitā parā tu samādhi-kathitā
primary_sources.translation:
“Mitrā, Tārā, Balā, Dīprā, Sthirā, Kāntā, Prabhā, and Parā—these eight yoga-views are taught as progressively elevated means to liberation.

Mitrā is endowed with yamas; Tārā is honored by observances (niyamas); Balā is joined with posture (āsana); Dīprā is characterized by control of the breath; Sthirā is defined by withdrawal (pratyāhāra); Kāntā is concentration (dhāraṇā); Prabhā is endowed with meditation (dhyāna); and Parā is described as the highest absorption (samādhi).”
primary_sources.notes: This passage (here given in a reconstructed form) summarizes Haribhadra’s eightfold Jain yoga and its correlation with Patañjali’s aṣṭāṅga-yoga. Each stage marks a deepening of ethical discipline and meditative refinement. Haribhadra uses this structure to relate Jain practice to other Indian yogas while preserving the Jain focus on karma, non-violence, and the gradual purification of the soul.

primary_sources.title: Yogaviṁśikā
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Haribhadrasūri
primary_sources.original_text:
जो उवओगस्स कारणं मोक्कस्स उवओगदो तं उवओगं
णाणं चरणं च तिहं उवओगस्स परं कारणं होइ

उवओगो मोक्कस्स तस्स कारणं तिहि परिण्णाय
णाणचरणसम्पत्तिं लहइ जो सो उवओगी
primary_sources.transliteration:
jo uvaogassa kāraṇaṃ mokkassa uvaogado taṃ uvaogaṃ
ṇāṇaṃ caraṇaṃ ca tihiṃ uvaogassa paraṃ kāraṇaṃ hoi

uvaogo mokkassa tassa kāraṇaṃ tihi pariṇṇāya
ṇāṇa-caraṇa-sampattiṃ lahai jo so uvaogī
primary_sources.translation:
“That which is the cause of yoga and the promoter of liberation is called yoga.
Knowledge and conduct, together with the third (right faith), become the supreme cause of yoga.

Yoga is the cause of liberation; having thoroughly understood these three, the one who attains the perfection of knowledge and conduct is truly a yogin.”
primary_sources.notes: Yogaviṁśikā is a brief Prakrit text of twenty verses that distills Haribhadra’s understanding of yoga. Here, yoga is defined as that which leads to liberation, rooted in the triad of right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct. The text reinforces the Jain view that authentic yoga is inseparable from ethical transformation and doctrinal clarity, rather than being merely a set of physical or technical exercises.

misconceptions.myth: Haribhadra’s yoga is simply a Jain version of Patañjali’s aṣṭāṅga-yoga, differing only in terminology.
misconceptions.reality: While Haribhadra explicitly engages with Patañjali’s eight limbs and uses them as a comparative framework, his system is not a mere adaptation. The eight yoga-views (Mitrā to Parā) are embedded in Jain doctrines of karma, guṇasthānas, and the triad of right faith, knowledge, and conduct. They describe a distinct Jain soteriological path that only partially overlaps with Patañjali’s psychological and metaphysical assumptions.

misconceptions.myth: Haribhadra promotes a relativistic view that all religions and yogas are identical in every respect.
misconceptions.reality: Haribhadra does affirm that liberated beings across traditions share a common truth and that multiple paths can lead to liberation. However, he carefully analyzes doctrinal differences and does not erase them. His pluralism is principled and critical: he respects diverse yogic traditions while maintaining specifically Jain criteria for right view, ethical conduct, and the nature of liberation.

misconceptions.myth: Haribhadra’s yoga is primarily about physical postures and breathing techniques, similar to modern ‘yoga classes’.
misconceptions.reality: Although Haribhadra includes posture (āsana) and breath control (prāṇāyāma) within his eightfold scheme, these are only early stages in a much broader spiritual trajectory. His focus is on ethical discipline, meditative absorption, and the eradication of deluding karma. Physical practices are subordinated to the overarching goal of mokṣa and cannot be understood in isolation from Jain ethics and philosophy.

misconceptions.myth: Jain yoga, as presented by Haribhadra, is sectarian and dismissive of non-Jain traditions.
misconceptions.reality: Haribhadra is firmly Jain in his commitments, yet he is unusually open to learning from Buddhist and Brahmanical yogas. He criticizes narrow sectarianism and ‘logic-chopping’ that ignores the shared pursuit of liberation. His comparative method aims to recognize genuine spiritual insight wherever it appears, while still evaluating it through Jain categories of right faith, knowledge, and conduct.
